h1: The 7 Best Compact Printers for Small Desks of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: seven compact printers for small desks, from Canon and HP inkjets to a Brother laser and a pocket thermal model.
summary: The Canon PIXMA TS4320 is the best compact printer for a small desk: a color inkjet that prints, copies and scans, with automatic duplex and wireless setup, for $50 to $100. The TS6520 adds an OLED display, the TR4720 an auto document feeder and fax, and the Brother HL-L2405W a toner that never dries.
intro: A desk-friendly printer is one you can forget about between jobs, and the footprint printed on the box rarely tells you that. Ink that dries out, a paper tray that sticks out, or a scanner lid you cannot open under a shelf can turn a small printer into a daily annoyance. Open the lid, pull the tray and feed the paper in your head before you buy.

We ranked seven compact models on paper, weighing body size, what each can do, how ink or toner behaves when idle, and the limits buried in spec lines. Rankings come from spec sheets and owner reports, not bench measurements. Five are inkjets, one is a laser and one is a pocket thermal printer, so running cost differs more than size.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS4320 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A small color all-in-one that still prints on both sides of the page.
products.description:
The TS4320 is a compact color inkjet that prints, copies and scans, and it adds automatic two-sided printing. It connects over wireless and works with the Canon PRINT mobile app. It sells for $50 to $100. Two-sided printing halves paper use, which keeps the paper tray smaller and the stack thinner on a cramped desk.

It ranks first because duplex printing is rare at this size. Against the TS6520 below, you give up the built-in OLED screen, which is a minor loss for most home users. Against the TS3720, it adds duplex for the same price bucket.

Buy it if you want one tidy machine for school and home paperwork. The caveat is that it handles only letter and A4 paper, with no legal or tabloid sizes, and inkjet ink can dry. Skip it if you print mostly black text and want toner.
products.idealFor: Students and remote workers needing a complete small printer.
products.skipIf: You print mostly black text and want toner.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: Same compact all-in-one idea, with a small screen for status checks.
products.description:
The TS6520 is a compact color inkjet all-in-one with a 1.42 inch OLED display and automatic duplex printing. Setup runs through the Canon PRINT app. It sells for $50 to $100. A small screen lets you see ink levels and errors on the machine, without picking up a phone.

It lands just behind the TS4320 because the screen is a convenience, not a capability, and both share the same feature set otherwise. The display does let you check ink or errors without reaching for a phone. Against the TR4720, it is slimmer but lacks a feeder.

Pick it if you like seeing status on the machine itself. The caveat is that the screen adds nothing else, and the phone app is still needed. Skip it if you are happy managing everything from a phone.
products.idealFor: Households who want status shown on the printer.
products.skipIf: You are happy managing everything from a phone.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: The only pick here with an automatic document feeder and fax.
products.description:
The TR4720 is a compact all-in-one that adds an auto document feeder and built-in fax to the usual print and scan duties. It pairs with mobile printing through the Canon PRINT app and sells for $50 to $100. A feeder scans a stack of pages without lifting the lid, which saves time on forms and receipts.

It sits third because the feeder adds bulk to a small desk, and the listing does not mention duplex printing. The tradeoff versus the TS4320 is paper handling for document handling. Against the DeskJet 4355, it offers a feeder and fax where the HP offers an ink trial.

It is a strong choice for people who scan multi-page forms or still send faxes. The caveat is the feeder body, so measure your shelf before ordering. Skip it if you rarely scan and want the smallest body.
products.idealFor: Home offices that scan or fax multi-page documents.
products.skipIf: You rarely scan and want the smallest body.

products.name: HP DeskJet 4355 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A compact HP all-in-one that leans on an ink subscription trial.
products.description:
The DeskJet 4355 is a compact color inkjet that prints, scans and copies, pairs through the HP Smart app and includes a three-month HP Instant Ink trial. It also lists AI-assisted print management features. It sells for $50 to $100. An ink trial lowers the early cost, since cartridges are billed by pages, not by the refill.

It ranks fourth because its appeal depends on the ink trial, and subscription ink can feel limiting once the trial ends. The Canon models list duplex printing; this listing does not. Against the TS3720, it adds an app and a trial but no duplex.

Choose it if you already use the HP app and want a gentle start on ink. The caveat is that you should read the Instant Ink terms before relying on the plan. Skip it if you dislike subscription ink programs.
products.idealFor: New printer owners wanting a gentle start on ink costs.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS3720 Wireless All-in-One Printer
products.verdict: The no-frills option for occasional printing in a tiny footprint.
products.description:
The TS3720 is a basic compact color all-in-one that prints, copies and scans, with wireless setup through the Canon PRINT app. It has a small, no-frills body and sells for $50 to $100. A smaller body fits shelves that a feeder-equipped model will not.

It ranks fifth because it lacks automatic duplex printing, which the TS4320 and TS6520 include. That is the main reason to step up a model within the same bucket. Against the TR4720, it is simpler and lighter but has no feeder.

Best for people who print a few pages a month. The caveat is manual two-sided printing, which takes extra steps and wastes time on bigger jobs. Skip it if you print long documents regularly.

products.name: Brother HL-L2405W Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: A print-only laser whose toner will not dry out on you.
products.description:
The HL-L2405W is a compact monochrome laser that prints only, with wireless mobile printing and Alexa compatibility. The listing notes that toner does not dry out between uses. It sells for $100 to $200. Laser toner is dry powder, so a printer that sits for weeks starts without clogged nozzles.

It ranks sixth purely because it cannot scan or copy and prints in black only, which is a bigger limit than the Canon all-in-ones. The tradeoff is reliability when the printer sits idle for weeks. Against the MT610Pro, it prints on standard paper and needs no special stock.

Choose it if you print mainly text and want a machine that works when you need it. The caveat is that scanning needs a second device. Skip it if you need color or a scanner.
products.idealFor: Text-heavy printing with long gaps between jobs.
products.skipIf: You need color or a scanner.

products.name: Inkless Portable Bluetooth Thermal Printer (MT610Pro)
products.verdict: Pocket-sized inkless printing for desks with no room for anything else.
products.description:
The MT610Pro is an inkless Bluetooth thermal printer at 300 DPI that handles 8.5 by 11 inch Letter and A4 paper. It pairs with iOS, Android and laptops, and it is the smallest, lightest device in this list. It sells for $50 to $100. Thermal printing heats special paper, so there is no cartridge to dry out.

It ranks last because it needs special thermal paper rather than standard copy paper, which adds a running cost and a supply to remember. That limit separates it from every other pick here. Against the HL-L2405W, it saves desk space but costs more per page.

Buy it for occasional printing where space is the only concern. The caveat is that thermal output is not meant for color work. Skip it if you want standard copy paper.
products.idealFor: Occasional printing where desk space is minimal.

whatMatters.detail: Inkjet, laser and thermal printers behave very differently. Inkjets handle color and photos but ink can dry out; lasers print sharp text and keep toner for months; thermal prints without ink but needs special paper. Check the listing title for the type, since it decides running costs. Five of the seven here are inkjets.

Duplex means the printer flips the sheet itself to print on both sides. It halves paper use and keeps stacks thin on a cramped desk. Look for the words auto duplex in the spec bullets; the TS4320 and TS6520 list it, while the TS3720 does not. Manual two-sided printing is slow and easy to get wrong.

Not every compact printer scans. The Brother HL-L2405W is print only, while the Canon all-in-ones scan and copy. If you scan multi-page paperwork, look for an automatic document feeder, as on the TR4720, rather than a flatbed alone. A flatbed handles single pages and books but is slow on stacks. A feeder adds bulk but saves time.

Most compact printers accept letter and A4 only. If you print legal documents or large posters, this matters. Check the listing for supported sizes and be wary of silence, since it usually means standard letter. Envelopes and labels may also need a rear feed. The Canon models here are letter and A4 only, and the MT610Pro lists the same two.

Inkjet cartridges can dry if the printer sits unused, leading to clogged heads. Laser toner does not dry out, as noted for the Brother. If you print rarely, a laser or thermal model may avoid wasted cartridges. A weekly short print keeps an inkjet healthy, and storing a printer in a dry place helps too.

cards.text: Prints in color and handles photos, but cartridges can dry out when idle. The Canon TS4320, TS6520, TS3720, TR4720 and HP DeskJet 4355 are inkjets.

cards.text: Monochrome laser prints sharp text, and toner does not dry out between uses. The Brother HL-L2405W is the laser pick.

faq.q: Will these printers fit under a shelf?
faq.a: Check the listing for exact dimensions, since scanner lids and paper trays need extra clearance. The thermal MT610Pro is the easiest to store. A TR4720 with its feeder is the tallest, and any model needs space behind it for the paper tray to extend.

faq.q: Do I need special paper for the thermal printer?
faq.a: Yes. The MT610Pro requires thermal paper, not standard copy paper, so plan for that running cost. Thermal sheets cost more than copy paper, and you cannot reuse a tray of ordinary stock.

faq.q: Is the Brother laser worth it over a Canon inkjet?
faq.a: Only if you print mostly black text and rarely use it. Toner does not dry out, but you lose color, scanning and copying. For a student or home worker who scans receipts, a Canon all-in-one is the more useful machine.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying a small printer?
faq.a: Ignoring paper size limits. These Canon models are letter and A4 only, so legal documents will not work. If you must print legal paper or large sheets, look for a model that lists those sizes or use a print shop.

faq.q: How do I set up the Canon models?
faq.a: Install the Canon PRINT app on your phone, then follow the wireless setup prompts. It works with iOS and Android. Keep the printer and phone on the same wireless network during setup, and update the app first.

faq.q: What happens to the HP Instant Ink trial?
faq.a: The three-month trial ends, after which you decide whether to subscribe. Read the terms first so you know the ongoing plan. A subscription can cost more than occasional cartridge refills if you print little.

finalTake: Buy the Canon PIXMA TS4320 for one tidy machine for school and home paperwork. Take the TS6520 if you like a status screen, the TR4720 if you scan or fax stacks, and the Brother HL-L2405W if you print text now and then. The TS3720 is the basic option, and the MT610Pro suits desks with no room. Check the shelf clearance first.
